title: Faith and the state
hookLine: Sikhs hold different views on religion and politics; the Gurus spoke truth to rulers

cards: Kings are tigers, and their officials are dogs. That isn't a protest sign. It's a line of scripture, a salok of Guru Nanak kept in the Guru Granth Sahib.
It says out loud, about the powerful, what the people under them might only whisper at home. The village clerk, the tax collector, the guard at the gate: the ones who knock at night.
Guru Nanak doesn't flatter them, and he doesn't flatter the throne behind them either. Truth, spoken to rulers.

teach.b: First, Guru Nanak's words. In the salok, in paraphrase: kings are tigers, their officials are dogs; they go and wake the sleeping to harass them. The servants of power wound people with their claws.
Blunt language about rulers, with no single king named. A few weeks ago, this path heard the Babarvani, his hymns on an invasion, which call the invading host a wedding party of sin.
The salok turns the same honesty on ordinary rule. Second, the throne facing the temple.
Tradition says Guru Hargobind wore two swords, miri and piri, worldly authority and spiritual authority, and built the Akal Takht, the Throne of the Timeless One, facing the Harmandir Sahib.
The message Sikhs draw from it: faith has something to say to power, and doesn't bow to it. Third, honest disagreement. Sikhs today hold different views on how faith and politics should meet.
Some see miri-piri as a call to stay engaged in public life, as Sikhs, together. Others keep faith out of party politics and put it into service and conscience instead.
Both draw on the same Gurus, and the tradition holds room for both. Fourth, what they share. Speaking truth to rulers isn't the same as wanting to rule.
The Gurus' words name injustice plainly, without flattery and without hatred.
It can be as large as a hymn about an invasion, or as small as one honest sentence at a city council, in an office, at a family table where one person's word is law.

how: Sikhs sing Guru Nanak's hymns and saloks on rulers, including the Babarvani, as part of the Guru Granth Sahib and look to the Akal Takht in Amritsar as a seat of temporal authority; Sikhs differ on how directly faith should engage in politics.

games.q: what does “faith and the state” mean?
o: a ruler's right to command a faith's beliefs
a promise to obey any ruler without question
how faith speaks honestly to those in power

games.q: truth to rulers: tap the pairs.
p: kings are tigers, in Guru Nanak's salok

s: Guru Nanak's salok compares kings to tigers and their officials to dogs
blunt words about the powerful, kept inside scripture.
all Sikhs agree on how faith and politics should meet
Sikhs hold different views, and both draw on the same Gurus.
speaking truth to rulers means wanting to rule
the Gurus named injustice plainly, without flattery and without hatred.

games.q: a powerful official in your town wants public praise for a rule that is hurting poor families. what do the Gurus' words point toward?
o: name the harm plainly, without flattery and without hatred.
games.why: Guru Nanak called kings tigers and their officials dogs, and Sikhs keep those words in scripture. truth to rulers.

practice: Bring to mind a place where power sits over you, a boss, an office, a rule, a family elder, and ask whether one honest thing there needs saying.
Don't version a speech; find the one sentence and turn it over, breath by breath, until it's both true and kind. If you pray, ask for courage in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Faith and the state. Sikhs hold different views on how they meet, and the Gurus, from the Babarvani to the Akal Takht, spoke truth to rulers. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: worldly authority and spiritual authority, the pair tradition links to Guru Hargobind's two swords.

carryVoice: Your line: truth to rulers. No flattery, no hatred, just the plain word. See you tomorrow.
